svg.title: Deciding the ERP migration tier by tier: the web tier can move, the application tier only with its database
svg.desc: The web tier is stateless and tolerant, so it moves to the cloud behind anycast. The application tier makes forty queries per transaction and needs sub-millisecond access to the database, so it moves only together with it. The database holds four terabytes and 1.2 million transactions a day under a fifteen-minute recovery point objective, so it stays where it is or moves as a single unit. The per-transaction latency budget shows how much room each move consumes.
svg.text: One ERP, three tiers, three different answers
The question is never "should the ERP go to the cloud" — it is which tier can survive the distance, and which cannot
DECIDE PER TIER
web tier
stateless, tolerant
MOVES
anycast or GSLB in front,
100 ms budget is enough
application tier
40 queries per txn
WITH DB
moves only as a unit with
the database it talks to
database tier
4 TB · 1.2 M txn/day
STAYS
RPO 15 min and residency,
replication measured, not assumed
PER-TRANSACTION LATENCY BUDGET · 200 ms allowed end to end
user ↔ web 40 ms
web ↔ app 4 ms · app ↔ db 2 ms
render 30 ms
margin 124 ms — this is what a migration may spend
Move the database alone and every one of the 40 queries pays 35 ms twice: 2.8 s, against a 200 ms budget.
The margin above is 124 ms, which is one and a half round trips. The arithmetic, not the vendor, sets the architecture.
CONNECTION MODEL, CHOSEN BY DETERMINISM
web ↔ users: Internet is acceptable — the web tier is stateless and retries are cheap
app ↔ db: dedicated circuit or same-region placement — 2 ms is not negotiable
db replication: dedicated path with measured loss; a 15-minute RPO is a bandwidth and latency claim
The order that survives audit
1 · measure the round-trip count per transaction, in production, not in the diagram
2 · move the stateless tier first; it is reversible in a weekend and proves the path
3 · keep the stateful pair co-located until the application can be made less chatty
4 · write the latency and loss ceilings into the circuit contract, with a breach clause
5 · rehearse the return path before the forward one — an untested way back is not a plan
Steps 1 and 5 cost nothing and decide whether the other three are affordable.
The rest of the migration is procurement and scheduling.
What the network team must hand over
a measured RTT matrix between every pair of sites and regions
the same matrix under load, at peak hour, not at 3 a.m.
per-path loss and jitter, because the ERP is chatty and TCP hides neither
the replication bandwidth actually available after every other tenant
the failure behaviour: what the path does when the primary circuit dies
Numbers, not adjectives. "Low latency" is not a handover.
The temptation is a single decision for "the ERP". The work is three decisions that happen to share a name.
